title.narrative: NIHR HPSR-CA - Intersectoral policy coalitions to improve early childhood development in Argentina and Ghana

description.narrative:
Intersectoral action is key to improving early childhood development, yet major knowledge gaps persist about how intersectoral policies interact with multi-level governance systems; how to engage communities, civil society, and children; and which factors enhance stakeholder coalitions and sustainability. Few models of intersectoral action have been developed from lower- and middle-income countries (LMICs). In a previous project called 'Children in All Policies', or CAP-2030, Argentina and Ghana explored intersectoral responses to shared challenges around early childhood development including child poverty, malnutrition, and limited participation of children in policy processes. These countries’ differing governance systems and levels of political prioritisation of early childhood development provide an opportunity to compare the development of intersectoral coalitions and their integration, coherence, and accountability.
This prospective policy analysis will assess a participatory, data-driven intervention to improve intersectoral early childhood development policy for children aged 0-8 years at sub-national level in five localities each in Argentina and Ghana. The five-stage intervention is designed to redress common pitfalls of intersectoral action for health by using inclusive issue framing; deliberate co-production with public and non-public-sector actors, including children; and collaborative resource generation. The research will take place from November 2024 to October 2029 and will be undertaken by University College London (UCL, UK), UCL Institute for Global Health (UK), Ghana Health Services (Ghana), Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection (Ghana), Center for Learning and Childhood Development (Ghana) and the Latin American Faculty of Social Sciences (FLACSO, Argentina).

The project has 4 objectives:
1. Explore how typologies of intersectoral action evolve in the context of differing political and fiscal power-sharing arrangements. 2. Investigate whether intermediate process indicators of collaboration and partnership are aligned with intersectoral policy coherence, and integration, and effects on early childhood development indicators. 3. Analyse how the engagement of non-governmental actors including civil society, communities and children can be maximised using inclusive issue framing and participatory data systems. 4. Promote institutionalised learning and increase stakeholders’ knowledge of and self-efficacy to engage in intersectoral policy processes.
